subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 11 of Year 3 Computing at Ehel Academy. Even though the unit is called Be a data designer, it is really all about spreadsheets. A spreadsheet is a computer program that shows data neatly in a table of little boxes. Each box is called a cell. You already meet tables every day: a class register, a football league table, or a bus timetable at the station are all data laid out in rows and columns.

First, what a spreadsheet is made of: rows that go across, columns that go up and down, and cells where a row and a column cross. Every cell has an address, like B5, from its column letter and row number. Second, that data can be formatted as Text, Number, Date or Currency, and that the format tells us what we can do with the data. Third, to choose the right data to answer a question by selecting the correct cells, and that we can only do sums on numbers and money, not on words or dates.
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 3 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Say that a spreadsheet shows data in a table of rows, columns and cells.
Give the cell address of a cell using its column letter and row number (for example B5).
Point to the active cell and the Name Box in a spreadsheet.
Enter data into a spreadsheet, with headings in the first row.
Choose the right format for data: Text, Number, Date or Currency.
Explain that we can do sums on Number and Currency data, but not on Text or Date data.
Choose and select the right cells (a range, like B2:B4) to answer a question.

concepts.title: What is a spreadsheet? Rows, columns and cells
concepts.explanation:
A spreadsheet shows data in a table. The table is made of rows (they go across, left to right, and each one has a number) and columns (they go up and down, and each one has a letter). Where a row and a column cross, you make a cell, and data goes inside the cell. The top row usually holds the headings that tell us what each column is about.

What does this data mean? Is it easy to read?
concepts.example: That is why we use a spreadsheet — it keeps our data neat and tidy. You see at once that the table is much easier to understand.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you find a single cell where a named row and column cross? Can you point to a row and a column correctly (across versus up-and-down)? Do not worry about addresses yet — that is next.

concepts.title: Cell addresses and the active cell
concepts.explanation:
Every cell has an address, so we can say exactly which box we mean. The address is the column letter first, then the row number — for example B5 means column B, row 5. When we click a cell it becomes the active cell and gets a dark border. The Name Box (a little box just above the top-left of the sheet) shows the address of the active cell.

Imagine our class is a grid. If I say 'third row, second seat', everyone knows exactly which chair I mean. A spreadsheet does the same thing with a letter and a number. Put your finger on A3.
concepts.example: What is in B4? Where is Leila's age?
concepts.checkYourself: Can you find a cell from its address, and give the address of a cell you point to? A common slip is writing the number first (like 3A) — gently point at the Name Box rule. Does you always write the letter before the number?

concepts.title: Entering data in a real spreadsheet
concepts.explanation:
Now we put our data into a real spreadsheet using LibreOffice Calc. We click a cell, type, and press Enter to move down. We always put the headings in the first row, then the data underneath.

When they can predict it before you click, they have understood addresses. Open LibreOffice Calc on the projector.
concepts.example: Point to the parts using child words: the columns are labelled with letters along the top (A, B, C), the rows are numbered down the side (1, 2, 3), and the Name Box in the top-left corner shows the address of the active cell. Click a few cells and you can read the address in the Name Box each time.
concepts.checkYourself: Does each name line up with the correct age on the same row? Do the headings go in row 1?

concepts.title: Formatting cells: Text, Number, Date, Currency
concepts.explanation:
A spreadsheet lets us choose how our data looks. This is called the format. The format is like the clothes the data wears. Money wears a dollar sign.

Try it: Fast finishers can format the fruit stall on screen.

Check yourself: Can you know that a code with letters and numbers is Text, not Number? Can you select a group of cells before choosing a format? Can you match data to the right format?
concepts.example: A date wears slashes between the day, month and year. A number is bare, ready for sums.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you know that a code with letters and numbers is Text, not Number? Can you select a group of cells before choosing a format? Can you match data to the right format?

concepts.title: Choosing the right data to solve a problem
concepts.explanation:
We keep data so we can answer questions with it. Different questions need different data.

Try it: If time allows, you type the bakery table into LibreOffice Calc and practise selecting each range.

Check yourself: Can you know we can only add Number or Currency data? Can you pick the correct column for a question?
concepts.example: To answer a question we select just the cells we need — a group of selected cells is called a range, written like B2:B4 (which means from B2 down to B4). The format is a clue: we can only do sums on Number and Currency data, never on Text or Date.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you know we can only add Number or Currency data? Can you pick the correct column for a question?

debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: Rows and columns get swapped all the time. Keep using the arm sweep and the rhyme: rows go across, columns go down.

debugging.symptom: The number comes first in an address, like 3A.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: The column letter always comes first, then the row number, so it is A3. Point to the letters along the top and the numbers down the side.

debugging.symptom: A code like FRU001 or a phone number is a Number.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: It has digits, but we never add it up, so it is Text. Use the test: would you ever add these together?

debugging.symptom: Any data can be added up.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: We can only do sums on Number and Currency data. We cannot add words (Text) or days (Date). Try adding two names out loud to show it makes no sense.

debugging.symptom: The heading is part of the data.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: The headings (row 1) are labels that name each column; they are not one of the ages or prices. When we add a column, we do not include the heading cell.

debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: Choosing Currency does not make the price bigger or smaller; it only changes how it looks (it adds a $). The value is the same.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

Can we add up data that is Text, like names? Which two formats CAN we add up?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: No, we cannot add up Text. We can only add up Number and Currency data.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in formatting cells: text, number, date, currency, and give one example of your own.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
A spreadsheet lets us choose how our data looks. This is called the format. The format is like the clothes the data wears. Money wears a dollar sign.

Try it: Fast finishers can format the fruit stall on screen.

Check yourself: Can you know that a code with letters and numbers is Text, not Number? Can you select a group of cells before choosing a format? Can you match data to the right format?

project.title: Unit 11 Project: Be a Data Designer
project.brief: Bring together everything from Be a Data Designer into one finished piece of work you can show and explain.
steps: Plan first: write down what your be a data designer project has to do before you build anything.
Build the smallest version that does one of those things, and run it.
Add one feature at a time, testing after each one.
When something breaks, change one thing, run it again, and note what fixed it.
Check your work against every success criterion below before you call it finished.
successCriteria: I have five friends, one on each row.
I chose the right format for each column.
My dates look like dates, and my money has a $.
I can give the cell address of any box, letter first.

I can choose and select the right cells (a range, like B2:B4) to answer a question.
